clue.text: Saints ace playing around with back from rugby team

indicators.note: letters that are playing around are fooling about out of their proper order
the back of a word is its last letter, so only that one is taken

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
W is the standard abbreviation for with
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A rugby side's ace kicker, playing for the Saints, lines up alongside a back from the team.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like rugby throughout, but the answer is a football club; only the last word, team, is the definition. Swansea City is a Welsh club playing in the English football league.
explanation.definitionFit: Swansea City is a professional football club, so it is an example of a sporting side.

clue.text: Welcomed old-fashioned instrument breaking down

indicators.note: something breaking into a word splits it open and sits inside

blocks.note: a lute is a plucked string instrument of the Renaissance
feeling down is feeling sad

explanation.surface: Someone greeted with a fanfare on an antique instrument that promptly breaks down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down' looks like the instrument failing, but it is the mood word that gets split open.
explanation.definitionFit: To salute someone is to greet them with a gesture of respect, so saluted means welcomed.

clue.text: Match experience entertains half of Kopites?

indicators.note: a host who entertains has guests inside the house, so one word holds another
taking only half of a word means the back half is cut away

blocks.note: age brings experience; one word can stand for the other
Kopites are Liverpool fans, and Liverpool are known as the Reds

explanation.surface: A football match experience laid on for some of the Liverpool fans on the Kop.
explanation.walkthrough: The Kop is the famous home stand at Liverpool's Anfield ground, and Liverpool are nicknamed the Reds; the question mark flags that Kopites stands for REDS before halving.
explanation.definitionFit: Two accounts that match are in accord, so the verb agree is a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: One who may give credit after second slight

indicators.note: what comes after something follows it, so the earlier-printed piece is placed later in the answer

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a lender gives credit, i.e. loans money

explanation.surface: A small-print warning that someone might give you credit only after a brief delay.
explanation.walkthrough: The long phrase reads as the definition, but it is wordplay; 'slight' at the end is the definition, and the abbreviation comes first because the clue says the lender follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: A slight figure is thin and delicate, which is what slender describes as an adjective.

clue.text: Debt, the entire amount changing hands, cockney gathers

indicators.note: left and right are the two hands, so one hand letter is swapped for the other
a London cockney drops initial aitches, so the opening H is lost

blocks.note: all is the entire amount; its two L (left) letters each become R (right)
one who gathers news hears it; spoken by a cockney it becomes 'EARS

explanation.surface: A cockney collects a debt as the full sum passes from one person to another.
explanation.walkthrough: L and R stand for left and right, the two hands. A cockney is a working-class Londoner, whose accent famously drops the H at the start of words.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrears are money owed and overdue, so the plural noun names an outstanding debt.

clue.text: Patient, going off gluten after visiting doctor free from runs

indicators.note: food going off has gone bad, and spoiled letters fall out of order
being free from something means having it taken away

blocks.note: someone visiting is in
DR is the abbreviation for doctor
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs, which is removed
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A hospital patient gives up gluten after a trip to a doctor who has cured their diarrhoea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patient' looks like a noun for a sick person, but it is the adjective, and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An indulgent person is tolerant and lenient towards others, much like someone patient with faults.

clue.text: Maybe Boris, you once heard, wrong to carry the case for Lamont

indicators.note: a case is the outer shell, so only the outside letters are kept
in a down entry, a word that carries another bears it on top

blocks.note: ye is the archaic form of you, as people once spoke it
the first and last letters of the name
a sin is a wrong

explanation.surface: A Boris of politics, you may hear, wrongly made the case for Chancellor Norman Lamont.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe Boris' points at Boris Johnson, but the Boris meant is Boris Yeltsin, Russia's first president. Norman Lamont was a British Chancellor of the Exchequer in the 1990s.
explanation.definitionFit: Boris Yeltsin was the Russian president, so he is one example of a person called Boris.

clue.text: On reflection, I appreciate that beer finally gets moved for free

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror shows things back to front
the closing letter is moved to a new spot, rearranging the word

blocks.note: ta is British slang for thanks
lager is a type of beer

explanation.surface: A drinker, thinking it over, is grateful the beer has finally been shifted at no charge.
explanation.walkthrough: TA, informal British for thank you, is what you say when you appreciate something. In LAGER the last letter moves up two places to make LARGE.
explanation.definitionFit: An escaped prisoner at large is still on the loose, so the phrase means free.

clue.text: 50-50 in a game for non-specialists

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the Roman numeral for 50, twice over
rounders is a British bat-and-ball game, rather like baseball

explanation.surface: An evenly balanced contest is a game suited to amateurs rather than experts.
explanation.walkthrough: 50-50 suggests even odds, but it is two Roman fifties. They sit between A and the game.
explanation.definitionFit: All-rounders have skills in many areas, especially in cricket, rather than specialising in one.

clue.text: The French backing Germany on free peppers

indicators.note: a backer stands behind, so this piece comes after the next one
one thing on another in an across entry is placed after it

blocks.note: to rid is to free
D is the international vehicle code for Germany
les is French for 'the' before a plural noun

explanation.surface: France supporting Germany on a free trade deal in spices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peppers' looks like the vegetable or spice, but here it is a verb: to pepper with shot is to riddle with holes.
explanation.definitionFit: To riddle something with bullets is to pepper it, so both verbs mean to pierce repeatedly.

clue.text: Cook grins wrapping as well as covering meat in large pile

indicators.note: to cook something is to work it into a new form
a wrapper goes all round its contents
in a down entry, a piece covering another sits above it

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
and means as well as
ham is a meat

explanation.surface: A cook smiles while wrapping and covering a mound of meat in the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: A pile is an old word for a grand house. Sandringham House in Norfolk is a private country home of the British royal family.
explanation.definitionFit: A pile is informal British for a stately home, and Sandringham is a large royal country house.

clue.text: Drink after eleven at night? Time to stop it

indicators.note: a stopper goes into an opening and plugs it

blocks.note: eleven at night is late
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A coffee after eleven at night? Time to stop that habit.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'it' points back to the word for after eleven at night, which is plugged by the time abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A latte is a coffee made with lots of steamed milk, so it is a kind of beverage.

clue.text: Tight denims lady not enjoying male lust?

indicators.note: not enjoying something means going without it, so it is removed
tight is slang for drunk, and drunken letters stagger out of order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
M is the abbreviation for male, which is removed

explanation.surface: A woman in tight jeans who is not keen on attracting men's desire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tight' seems to describe the jeans but is the anagram signal; the question mark shows lust is an example of the answer, not a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Lust is one of the seven deadly sins in Christian teaching, so it is an example of the category.

clue.text: Pensioner with large rum bottles getting attention

indicators.note: to bottle something is to put it inside a container

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for large
rum is British slang for strange or odd
to have someone's ear is to have their attention

explanation.surface: An elderly drinker with plenty of rum bottles draws notice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the drink but is the adjective meaning odd, and 'bottles' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Old dear is affectionate British slang for an elderly woman, typically someone retired on a pension.

clue.text: Bringing about collapse of ceiling having been charged with just the thing

indicators.note: a collapsed structure falls into a jumble
something charged with a substance is filled with it

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
'it' means exactly what is wanted, as in 'that's it'

explanation.surface: A builder causing a ceiling to fall in and then being charged for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charged with' sounds like a criminal charge, but it means loaded or filled.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliciting a response is drawing it out or prompting it, which is bringing it about.

clue.text: Pilot admitting service is comparatively demanding

indicators.note: to admit someone is to let them inside

blocks.note: to pilot a vessel is to steer it
RN is the Royal Navy, one of the armed services

explanation.surface: An airline pilot letting customer service know that they are tougher to please.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords 'service' often means one of the armed forces; here the Royal Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: Stern means strict and exacting, and the comparative form expresses a greater degree of severity.

clue.text: Encourage uniform-free former prime minister wanting one in the end

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the last letter, a one, is missing

blocks.note: free of uniform means no U, U being uniform in the radio alphabet
Rishi Sunak was UK Prime Minister from 2022 to 2024

explanation.surface: Encouraging an ex-premier to give up the suit and tie for good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform-free' reads as one adjective but splits into NO plus U. The one lost from the end is the letter I, which looks like the numeral 1.
explanation.definitionFit: To nourish hopes or talent is to foster and promote them, a figurative sense close to encouraging.

clue.text: Separate cakes discovered with slight problem

indicators.note: dis-covered means having its covering removed, so the outer letters go

blocks.note: buns are small cakes
a hitch is a minor snag

explanation.surface: A baker finds a small problem with the cakes and has to sort them apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' means found in the surface, but cryptically it is read as uncovered, stripping the outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To unhitch two things is to unfasten them from each other, so the verb means to detach.

clue.text: Husband, Sky member, tipped product used for style

explanation.walkthrough: Sky is a British satellite broadcaster, which makes 'Sky member' look like an employee; it splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair gel is a styling product that holds a hairdo in place, so it is used for style.

clue.text: Pick up new art on coach

blocks.note: re means on, as in on the subject of
to coach is to train

explanation.surface: Collecting a new painting from the bus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pick up' and 'coach' suggest collecting something from a bus, but the first four words are the definition; art means a skill or craft.
explanation.definitionFit: To retrain is to learn fresh skills, so picking up a new craft or technique describes it.

clue.text: The compiler’s band, according to Spooner is like Slade and Suede

indicators.note: William Spooner was famed for swapping the opening sounds of words

blocks.note: the setter's band is MY RING; swapping the opening sounds gives these two syllables

explanation.walkthrough: Slade and Suede are British rock bands, so 'band' looks musical, but a band here is a ring. Slade and Suede share their final sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Words that end with matching sounds are said to rhyme, and the two band names chime at the end.

clue.text: Rated jam put on sandwiches

explanation.surface: A highly rated jam is spread on some sandwiches.

explanation.definitionFit: To rate someone, in informal British use, is to think highly of them, which is to admire them.

clue.text: Back in Amsterdam perhaps following the cycling race

letters cycling go round like a wheel, the front ones riding to the rear
one piece following another comes after it

blocks.note: taken as written; its letters rotate
taken as written

clue.text: Pep‘s zip not moving at this speed?

clue.text: My job location

clue.text: Acting with Chic exhausted The Edge

clue.text: Stressed as lit up lamp from abroad turned over
